SK2160 The clock is read from a static

A member reads DateTime.Now, DateTime.UtcNow, DateTime.Today or the DateTimeOffset equivalents from a static, so no caller and no test can give it a different time. Ships disabled; turn it on per path.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitynone
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS6354

Why

A static clock read is a dependency the signature does not mention and the call site cannot replace. Code that depends on it can only be tested by waiting — which is what produces the Thread.Sleep that SK8005 then reports — and by tests that pass in one time zone and fail in another. TimeProvider, .NET 8's answer, turns the read into an ordinary injected dependency: the test supplies the instant and the production path supplies TimeProvider.System.

Example

Instead of:

public bool IsExpired(Token token) => token.ExpiresAt < DateTime.UtcNow;

Write:

public bool IsExpired(Token token) => token.ExpiresAt < time.GetUtcNow();

When it does not fire

⚠ This ships `defaultSeverity: none`, and the measurement that decided it is not the one that was wanted. Run over Skala's own solution from a fresh Release binlog — a load carrying 10 CS diagnostics, every one of them CS9335 (the pattern is redundant, a warning), no CS errors, no AD0001 and no SK9030 — with the severity temporarily raised, the rule reports 6 findings across the whole first-party tree. Six cannot calibrate anything. That is the honest statement rather than a justification derived from it: a low count here is not evidence that the rule is quiet, it is evidence that Skala barely asks what time it is.

⚠ The number with content came from Vixen, and it is an argument for `none` rather than against it. Measured the same way from its own fresh binlog — a load of 159 CS diagnostics across 8 codes, no AD0001, no SK9030 — the rule reports 38, and every one is a true positive. 22 of the 38 sit in `*.Tests` projects, in helper methods that poll a deadline — code the exclusion below cannot reach, because xUnit has no class-level attribute and a helper carries none of its own. Vixen is a test subject and never a specification, so 38 does not set a severity either. What the two numbers establish between them is the shape of the risk: the population is large on a repository that has not adopted TimeProvider, most of it is test scaffolding that is untestable by design, and adoption is a decision a repository makes once rather than a defect it repairs line by line. Nothing available measures the case that would actually decide it. So the rule is opt-in exactly the way SK7010, SK7101 and SK6053 are, and Skala does not assert an architectural policy on evidence it does not have.

⚠ The whole analyzer withdraws where `System.TimeProvider` does not resolve. Below .NET 8 the repair this rule names does not exist, and a finding whose advice cannot be taken is noise with a citation. ⚠ The lookup is GetTypesByMetadataName, plural, because a repository may ship its own System.TimeProvider shim under #if !NET8_0_OR_GREATER — Serilog does. That is for the exclusion rather than the guard: where both a shim and the framework type exist, a body deriving from either is the designated place to read the real clock. A first account of this claimed the singular lookup returns null for the ambiguity and silently disabled the rule on Serilog; measured, that is false — the singular form returns the source symbol and the plural returns two.

Five members, and the constants deliberately are not among them. DateTime.Now, DateTime.UtcNow, DateTime.Today and the DateTimeOffset equivalents are clock reads; MinValue, MaxValue and default are constants, and reporting them would make every sentinel comparison a finding. Every type test requires the symbol to come from metadata, so a repository's own type called DateTime is never matched. DateTime.Now.Date is one finding rather than two, because Date is an instance property and the outer access is not itself a clock read.

⚠ A type deriving from `System.TimeProvider` is excluded, because somebody has to read the real clock. That is where the framework says it happens, and reporting the one read inside a provider would be reporting the repair the rule asks for. The base chain is walked, so an intermediate abstract provider is covered.

⚠ Test code is excluded outright, and that is what makes this rule disjoint from `SK8007` by construction rather than by filter. SK8007 reports a live clock consumed by an xUnit assertion; this rule never looks inside a test at all, so no read can carry both findings and neither declares supersedes. The exclusion reads the method's attributes and the containing type's, which covers a fixture's constructor and an MSTest or NUnit fixture's helpers. It does not cover a helper in an xUnit class, because xUnit has no class-level attribute to read — the residual measured above, and a stated gap rather than an oversight.

⚠ No fix, and `SK6053`'s argument is the reason unchanged. The repair is to take a TimeProvider as a dependency, which adds a constructor parameter and changes every call site and every registration. ADR-005 makes a Skala fix a minimal text-edit list against one file's original SourceText; an edit that changed the declaration and nothing else would break the build on the tool's advice, which is the one thing a fix may never do.

Configuration

  • dotnet_diagnostic.SK2160.severity (none by default; set it per path to enable)
